fact_en:
How do plants help break solid rocks into soil?

Plant roots grow into cracks in solid bedrock! They physically break the rock apart during the initial stages of soil formation.
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagtabang sa mga tanom sa pagbungkag sa hugot nga bato?

Motubo ang mga gamot sa tanom sa mga liki sa hugot nga bedrock! Pisikal nilang gibungkag ang bato sa sinugdanan sa paghimo og yuta.

findings.note: title_bis "Paghubas sa Gamot" for "Root Weathering". Cebuano `hubas` = to DRY UP / ebb (of water), never to weather or break down rock. The title announces "the drying-up of the root" — a different process from the one the card teaches (roots wedging into bedrock cracks and physically breaking it), and no Cebuano word for weathering/breaking-down appears in the title to correct it.

fact_en:
Why do moonquakes last so long on the Moon?

The Moon's solid, rocky body vibrates like a ringing bell when shaken, so moonquakes can last up to an hour!
fact_bis:
Ngano dugay ang moonquakes sa Bulan?

Ang solidong bato sa Bulan nag-vibrate sama sa kampana kung gikulob, mao nga ang moonquakes makaabot og usa ka oras!

findings.note: bis body: "Ang solidong bato sa Bulan nag-vibrate sama sa kampana kung gikulob" for EN "...vibrates like a ringing bell when shaken". Cebuano `kulob` = to turn face-down / overturn, not to shake (uyog, tay-og, kurog). The stated trigger for the bell-like ringing becomes flipping the Moon over, which is nonsense as a mechanism, and the card never restores the shaking/impact idea elsewhere.

fact_en: In 2019, people in Mindanao witnessed a partial solar eclipse! This amazing event happened when the moon moved and blocked the sun.
fact_bis: Niadtong 2019, nakakita ang mga tawo sa Mindanao og partial solar eclipse! Nahitabo ni sa dihang nibulag ang buwan sa adlaw.

findings.note: Body: "Nahitabo ni sa dihang NIBULAG ang buwan sa adlaw" for EN "happened when the moon moved and BLOCKED the sun". Cebuano bulag = to separate / part from, not to block or cover (that is mitabon / misalipod). The card therefore states the eclipse happened when the moon SEPARATED FROM the sun — the direction of the mechanism is reversed, and the blocking fact appears nowhere else on the card. A child asked why a solar eclipse happens would answer with the opposite of the truth.

fact_en:
What is a waxing crescent moon?

It happens right after the new moon when a small, sliver-shaped part of the moon finally gets illuminated!
fact_bis:
Unsa ang waxing crescent moon?

Mahitabo kini pagkahuman sa new moon kung usa ka gamay, hugis-sipit nga bahin sa buwan ang nagpakahayag!

findings.note: title_bis "Nagtubo nga Gasuklay" for "Waxing Crescent". Gasuklay is the TAGALOG moon-phase word for crescent; in Cebuano suklay = comb and the ga- prefix is the progressive aspect marker, so the title parses as "growing, is combing". Cebuano would use bag-ong subang / the English term. Tagalog-only vocabulary in the title, with the correct sense carried only by the English "waxing crescent moon" left in the body.

fact_en: Limestone caves can trap heavy carbon dioxide gas near the floor, which might suffocate you if you crawl inside!
fact_bis: Pwede mag-trap ug bug-at nga carbon dioxide gas duol sa salog ang limestone caves, nga makasul-ob kung magsulod ka nga nag-crawl!

findings.note: Body: "...carbon dioxide gas duol sa salog ang limestone caves, nga MAKASUL-OB kung magsulod ka nga nag-crawl!" EN = "which might SUFFOCATE you if you crawl inside". Cebuano sul-ob = TO WEAR (put on clothing); suffocate is makalumos / makahuot / makatuok. The one fact that makes the card a safety warning — the gas can kill you by suffocation — is replaced by nonsense ("can wear you") and is never restored anywhere on the card; the title only says "Kuyaw sa Langob" (cave danger) without naming the hazard. A child reads only that caves are somehow dangerous, and cannot answer what the trapped CO2 actually does.

fact_en: When a medium-sized star runs out of hydrogen fuel in its core, it expands and cools down to become a red giant!
fact_bis: Kung maubusan na sa hydrogen fuel sa core ang usa ka medium-sized nga bituon, molapad ug molamig kini aron mahimong red giant!

findings.note: title_bis "Red Giant gikan sa Sobra" = "Red Giant from EXCESS/SURPLUS", but the fact — stated correctly in the card's own body — is the reverse: "Kung MAUBUSAN na sa hydrogen fuel sa core ... mahimong red giant" (when it RUNS OUT of fuel). The title asserts the opposite driver of the very process the card teaches, and also drops "fuel" (title_en: "Red Giants from Fuel"). Lower severity than the word-swaps above since the body restores it, but the title as displayed states a reversed relationship.

fact_en:
Why should you never stare at the sun?

Looking at our closest star can permanently damage your retina and cause partial blindness!
fact_bis:
Ngano nga dili ka dapat mudunggo sa adlaw?

Ang pagtan-aw sa atong pinakaduol nga bituon makadaut permanente sa retina ug makapahinabo og partial nga pagkabulag!

findings.note: Body answer: "makadaut permanente sa retina ug makapahinabo og partial nga PAGKABULAG" for EN "cause partial BLINDNESS". This is the confirmed false friend: Cebuano bulag = TO SEPARATE / part ways (pagkabulag = a breakup); Cebuano for blind is buta, so blindness is pagkabuta. Nothing on the card restores "blindness" — the child gets "damages the retina and causes partial separation", and the actual consequence of staring at the sun is unrecoverable. (Note the same card's question also uses mudunggo = to dock/land for "stare", but the title "Ayaw Tutoka sa Adlaw" and the answer's "pagtan-aw" restore that one — the blindness word is the unrecoverable part.)

fact_en:
Where does the Tamaraw graze?

In Mindoro's high-altitude grasslands! This ecosystem was formed from the weathering of ancient volcanic rocks.
fact_bis:
Asa nag-graze ang Tamaraw?

Sa taas nga damuhan sa Mindoro! Nabuhat ang ecosystem gikan sa weathering sa daan nga bulkanikong bato.

findings.note: title_bis "Paghubas sa Bato" for title_en "Rock Weathering" — hubas = TO EBB / DRY UP / EVAPORATE (tubig mihubas), a completely different process from the physical/chemical break-up of rock. The body keeps the English "weathering" untranslated, so the title is the ONLY Cebuano gloss the child gets, and it teaches that weathering means rock drying up. Nothing in the card corrects it.

fact_en: If caught outside during a thunderstorm, crouch low in a ditch instead of standing under a tall, isolated tree!
fact_bis: Kung maapil ka sa gawas samtang nag-ulan og kilat, lingkodi ang imong lawas sa ubos sa usa ka lungag imbis nga magtindog ilawom sa taas, nag-inusara nga kahoy!

findings.note: "lingkodi ang imong lawas sa ubos sa usa ka lungag" — lingkod = TO SIT (the known false friend). English is "crouch low in a ditch" during a thunderstorm; crouching is pungko/duko. On a lightning-safety card the action IS the fact, and it is changed to sitting (the posture safety advice specifically avoids) with no correction anywhere in the card. The title compounds it: "Yuko Bangin" puts the child at a bangin (ravine/precipice), not the kanal/ditch of the English title.

fact_en:
How do scientists test minerals?

Geologists rub a mineral against an unglazed porcelain streak plate to see the color of its powder!
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagsulay sa mga mineral sa mga scientist?

Ang mga geologist nag-uyog sa mineral batok sa unglazed porcelain streak plate aron makita ang kolor sa iyang pulbos!

findings.note: "Ang mga geologist nag-uyog sa mineral batok sa unglazed porcelain streak plate" — uyog = TO SHAKE (this same corpus uses pag-uyog correctly for earthquake shaking, e.g. ffct-36311). English: "rub a mineral against a streak plate". Cebuano rub/scrape is kuskos/kiskis. The streak test's method is the entire fact of the card; a child answering "Unsaon pagsulay sa mga mineral?" would say scientists SHAKE the mineral at a plate, and no other sentence restores the rubbing.

fact_en: During extreme heatwaves, your body sweats to cool your skin. But if you don't replace fluids, this sweating can cause dangerous dehydration!
fact_bis: Sa grabe nga kainit, ang lawas magpahiyom aron mapabugnaw ang panit. Apan kung dili mapuli ang likido, mahimo kini magdala ug delikado nga dehydration!

findings.note: "ang lawas magpahiyom aron mapabugnaw ang panit" — pahiyom = TO SMILE. English: "your body sweats to cool your skin". Cebuano sweat is singot/gasingot. The card's whole mechanism (sweating cools you, so replace the lost fluid or you dehydrate) is gone: the Cebuano says the body SMILES to cool the skin, and nothing else in the card ever mentions sweat, so the link between the lost "likido" and dehydration is unrecoverable.

fact_en: A surprising result is a reason to repeat the trial! Don't stop and tell a story that has only one measurement behind it.
fact_bis: Ang nakurat nga resulta hinungdan nga balik-balikon ang eksperimento! Ayaw hunonga ug istorya nga usa ra ka sukod ang naa niini.

findings.note: title_bis "Balik Kabantug Resulta" for title_en "Repeat Surprising Results" — bantug/kabantug = FAMOUS, RENOWNED, not surprising (katingad-an/nakurat). The card's own body uses the correct word, "Ang nakurat nga resulta hinungdan nga balik-balikon ang eksperimento", which is the strongest evidence the title is the outlier. As a heading it states a different rule (repeat the famous result rather than the surprising one).
